topic: NEP 2020, RTE Act, NCF and Policies: Right to Education (RTE) Act 2009
description: This module provides a comprehensive breakdown of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009. It details the constitutional backing (Article 21A), statutory norms for schools and teachers (PTR, working hours), the role of School Management Committees (SMCs), and the strict legal prohibitions on screening, capitation fees, and corporal punishment.

key_points: 86th Amendment Act (2002): Inserted Article 21A in the Constitution of India, making education a Fundamental Right.
Article 21A: Mandates the State to provide free and compulsory education to all children in the age group of 6 to 14 years.
Enforcement: The RTE Act was passed by Parliament in 2009 and came into effect on April 1, 2010 (except in the state of Jammu & Kashmir).

Free and Compulsory: 'Free' means no child is liable to pay any kind of fee or charge. 'Compulsory' means it is the government's obligation to ensure admission, attendance, and completion of elementary education.
Zero Rejection Policy: No child can be denied admission based on lack of age proof, religion, caste, or background.

Age-Appropriate Admission: If a child above 6 years has never been to school, they must be admitted to an age-appropriate class (e.g., a 10-year-old goes to Class 5) and provided special training to catch up.
Section 17 (No Corporal Punishment): Strictly prohibits physical punishment and mental harassment. It legally enforces a 'fear-free' environment.
No Screening & No Capitation Fee: Schools cannot conduct interviews of parents or children for admission, nor can they charge hidden capitation fees.
25% Reservation: Section 12(1)(c) mandates all private, unaided schools to reserve 25% of their entry-level seats for children from Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) and disadvantaged groups.
Pupil-Teacher Ratio (PTR): 30:1 for Primary (Classes 1-5) and 35:1 for Upper Primary (Classes 6-8). If primary school enrollment exceeds 200, the ratio must not exceed 40:1.
Minimum Working Days: 200 days for Primary; 220 days for Upper Primary.
Instructional Hours: 800 hours per academic year for Primary; 1000 hours for Upper Primary.
Teacher Working Hours: A minimum of 45 working hours per week (including preparation time).
School Management Committee (SMC): Mandates the formation of SMCs in all government and aided schools. 75% of SMC members must be parents/guardians, and 50% of the total members must be women.

questions.question: Which Constitutional Amendment Act led to the insertion of Article 21A, making elementary education a Fundamental Right in India?
questions.explanation: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2002 added Article 21A, which guaranteed free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14. This formed the legal basis for the RTE Act of 2009.

questions.question: According to the RTE Act 2009, what are the minimum number of working hours per week mandated for a teacher?
questions.explanation: The RTE Act officially mandates a minimum of 45 working hours per week for teachers. This time includes both actual classroom teaching and preparation time.

questions.question: A 10-year-old child from a marginalized community who has never attended any school comes to a government school for admission. According to the RTE Act 2009, what must the school principal do?

options.A: Admit the child to Class 1, as they have no prior educational background.
options.B: Refuse admission and advise the parents to send the child to an open school.
options.C: Admit the child to Class 5 (age-appropriate class) and arrange for special remedial training to bridge the learning gap.
options.D: Conduct an entrance test to decide which class the child deserves to be placed in.

questions.explanation: A critical provision of the RTE Act is 'Age-Appropriate Admission'. A child who has dropped out or never been to school must be placed in a class corresponding to their chronological age, accompanied by special training to help them integrate.

questions.question: A reputed private school demands a 'donation' and conducts an interview of both the child and the parents before granting admission to Grade 1. Under which provisions of the RTE Act 2009 is this illegal?

options.B: Prohibition of Capitation Fee and Screening Procedures
options.C: Prohibition of Private Tuition by Teachers

questions.explanation: The RTE Act strictly outlaws any screening tests or interviews for elementary admissions, and the collection of capitation fees (donations). Admissions must be done transparently, often via lottery for oversubscribed schools.

questions.question: The RTE Act mandates the creation of a School Management Committee (SMC) in government schools. To ensure democratic community participation and prevent bureaucratic monopoly, what specific demographic composition does the Act require for the SMC?

options.A: 100% of the members must be local government officials and politicians.
options.B: At least 75% of the members must be parents or guardians of students in the school, and 50% of the total members must be women.
options.C: 50% of members must be teachers and 50% must be students.
options.D: The committee must consist solely of external educational NGO workers.

questions.explanation: The RTE Act decentralized school governance by giving power to the immediate stakeholders: the parents. Requiring 75% parent representation and 50% female representation ensures that decisions regarding school development and funds are driven by the community that the school serves.
